newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Silver lining in rand fall - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Silver lining in rand fall - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

To some it might appear that one is being like Voltaire's Dr Pangloss, the irrepressible optimist who believed that all is best in the best of all possible worlds, in saying that the currency upheavals this year have been for the best.
Admittedly last week's movement was overdone and precipitate, but there is every reason to expect some degree of consolidation to happen.

The rand plummeted to a low of 4.77 to the dollar on the last day of October in contrast to the 4.70 to the dollar that I personally had been projecting for the end of the year, but which was the most extreme forecast by economists in the country.

There was a seven cent recovery in the day and the week ended at 4.69 to the dollar. Further strengthening of the rand down to 4.60 is possible in coming weeks and the projected end-year 4.70 is still feasible.

Whatever the final outcome there will be a sizeable depreciation of the rand over the year from the 3.65 at the beginning which will have effectively wiped out the overvaluation of the rand that the South African economy has been labouring with, certainly since 1989. Indeed the rand will have been pushed into being undervalued.

Of course there is no precision to the matter of assessing over- and under-valuation in that there is no immutable law of economic nature to provide the basis of measurement. However, as the crude rule of thumb the comparative purchasing power parity principle does provide a rough and ready means of assessment.
As Dr Tietmeyer once said, you might not be able to define an elephant but you will certainly recognise one, and similarly an overvalued currency.

At 3.65 rand a number of experts had assessed the rand to be about 15 percent overvalued; namely a "correct" value would be 4.20 rand. Allowing for a further seven percent differential price movement during the year a "correct" end-year rand would be 4.50. The projected 4.70 rand thus implies a 4.5 percent undervaluation.

Although this will no doubt be dissipated fairly rapidly with an escalation in internal working costs it certainly is better having this than struggling with an overvalued currency. It need hardly be said that the standard part of any IMF rescue package is a devaluation of the currency.

The very strength of the rand during 1995 was proving to be a stifling stranglehold on the economy, the repercussions of which were to be seen in the economic slowdown in 1996. If we are to achieve a three percent GDP growth this year it is because of the strong recovery in the agricultural sector.
The export sector is the principal engine of growth and the inhibiting strength of the rand last year was well exemplified in the gold mining sector.

Working profits of the member mines of the Chamber of Mines dropped from 6.1 billion rand in 1994 to 3.4 billion rand in 1995. A recovery to some 4.8 billion rand this year is possible but only because of the depreciation of the rand.

Generally the drop in the rand has been attributed to a lack of confidence in South Africa but stated with varying degrees of stridency and desperation. And extraordinary corrective measures have been sought and promoted, including raising interest rates, abandoning exchange controls and seeking IMF support.
Unfortunately this leaves the impression that the touchstone of measures is the satisfaction of American bank boardrooms rather than the domestic interests of the South African economy.

What has to be recognised is that the weakness of the rand is not simply a reflection of a lack of confidence. The currency has swung from being exceptionally strong and stable during 1995 when the dollar itself was weak but basically because the large deficit on current account was amply covered by a surplus on capital account. Reserves rose and the currency was in net demand.

This situation has been reversed in 1996 largely because of the running down of the trade liabilities, that is in effect delayed payment of the import excesses of 1995. The capital account has as a result been either negative or at best neutral while the current account has remained negative. Reserves have moved down continuously during the year and this has made the currency vulnerable to speculative attack.
The result has been a healthy correction with wholly beneficial economic benefits.

The economy continues to be subject to the restraints of stringent monetary policy in pursuit of the Holy Grail of price stability, and the general thrust of the overly vaunted macro-economic strategy is deflationary. In this restrictive economic environment the only escape valve is the foreign exchange rate. That the currency has fallen out of bed should be more a matter of relief than the cause of lamentation and hand wringing.
Like a supertanker the balance of payments situation should swing round slowly with stimulus to the export industries and with a degree of currency protection afforded to domestic industries.

The prospects for the capital account are also favourable with short-term liabilities having been reduced to more moderate levels. The rate of depreciation should therefore slow down distinctly, which could feed back on the balance of payments in encouraging a new foreign portfolio investments.
And with an improving domestic economy we may even become attractive for foreign direct investment, which has been authoritatively linked to market growth and opportunity.
Who knows?
The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
